quiz.p: Priya, a girl in Class 3, sees two lines. One looks longer, but a ruler shows both are 8 cm. What is this called?
quiz.why: When what we see is different from what is really there, as a ruler shows, it is called an illusion. Picking 'bad eyesight' is a common idea, but illusions fool people with perfect eyes too.

quiz.p: Where does the mistake in an optical illusion happen?
opts: In the eyes, which catch the light wrongly
In the brain, which uses a clue and gets the answer wrong
quiz.why: The eyes catch the light correctly. The brain works out sizes and shapes from clues, and an illusion is when a clue leads it to the wrong answer.

quiz.p: Why does a strip near the narrow end of railway-track drawings look longer?
opts: The brain reads that end as far away, and makes far things look bigger
That strip is closer to your eyes
The pencil lines make it grow
quiz.why: Lines that come together are a clue for 'far away'. The brain makes a far thing that still looks big seem even bigger.

quiz.p: In the arrow-lines test, which result shows that the open fins fooled Nandini?
opts: Her plain copy was 10 cm and her open-fin copy was 12 cm
Her plain copy was 12 cm and her open-fin copy was 12 cm
quiz.why: Her plain copy shows she copies well. The extra 2 cm on the open-fin copy came from the fins. If both copies were 12 cm, she simply copies long.

quiz.p: In the arrow-lines test, why does everyone copy a plain line too?
opts: To see how well each person copies anyway, so we know how much the fins added
quiz.why: The plain line is the fair comparison. Without it, we could not tell an illusion from ordinary copying mistakes.

quiz.p: After measuring the arrow lines and knowing they are equal, what do most people see?
opts: The open-fin line still looks longer
The arrowhead line now looks longer
quiz.why: Knowing the answer changes what you believe, but not much what you see. The seeing part of the brain keeps its own answer.

quiz.p: Why does a flip book seem to move?
opts: The drawings slide across the page
The brain joins still pictures shown quickly into movement
quiz.why: Each page is still. When pictures with small differences come quickly one after another, the brain builds smooth movement. This is apparent motion.

quiz.p: Max Wertheimer flashed two lines of light, one after the other. People saw one line moving. Why did this show that 'persistence of vision' is wrong?
opts: Blurring on the eye would show two lines at once, not one line travelling
quiz.why: If pictures only stayed on the eye and blurred, people would see two lines together. Seeing one line move across the empty space showed the brain makes the movement.

quiz.p: Rolling one pea between crossed fingertips often feels like two peas. What does this show?
quiz.why: The brain decides that the outer sides of two fingers touching a small thing must mean two things. This is an illusion of touch, called Aristotle's illusion.

quiz.p: A peacock pansy butterfly has big round eyespots on their wings. How can the eyespots help the butterfly?
opts: They help the butterfly see better
They can startle a hungry bird, who may back away
quiz.why: Eyespots are not real eyes. To a bird, two big round spots can look like a dangerous animal's eyes, so the bird may back away.

quiz.p: A circle shaded light at the top looks like a bump. You turn the page upside down. What happens?
opts: It still looks like a bump
quiz.why: The brain expects light from above. Turned over, the light part is at the bottom, so the surface seems to face down: a dent.

quiz.p: Which is the best way to find out if two lines are really the same length?
quiz.why: Looking harder does not switch off an illusion, and other people are usually fooled the same way. A ruler cannot be fooled by fins or neighbours.

items.p: What is an illusion?
opts: When what you see or feel is different from what is really there
A picture that is badly drawn
items.why: An illusion is when what you see, hear or feel is different from what is really there, as a ruler or a test shows. It happens to people with healthy eyes. Picking 'eyes are broken' is a common idea, but illusions fool almost everyone.

items.p: In the railway-track drawing, two equal paper strips lie across the tracks. Which one looks longer?
opts: The one near the narrow end, where the lines come together
The one near the wide end
items.why: The narrow end looks far away. The brain makes a far thing that still looks big seem bigger, so that strip looks longer.

items.p: Which two parts of your body work together to see?
items.why: The eyes catch light and send signals. The brain works out what the signals mean: sizes, shapes, distances and movement.

items.p: A film at a cinema hall is really made of...
items.why: A film is a row of still pictures called frames. Most cinema films show 24 every second. The brain joins them into movement.

items.p: If you have good eyesight, illusions cannot fool you.
items.why: False. Illusions fool people with perfect eyesight too, because the mistake is in how the brain uses clues, not in the eyes.

items.p: A ruler is a fair way to check whether two lines are the same length.
items.why: True. A ruler does not compare a line with its fins or neighbours, so the fins cannot fool it.

items.p: Your sense of touch can be fooled, as well as your sight.
items.why: True. With crossed fingers, one pea rolled between the fingertips often feels like two.

items.p: One still picture in a film or a flip book is called a ____.
items.why: Films and flip books are made of frames. Shown quickly, frames look like movement.

items.p: The brain expects light to come from ____, because the Sun and most lamps are there.
items.why: That is why a circle shaded light at the top looks like a bump, and turned over, like a dent.

items.p: Match each illusion to the clue that fools the brain.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each illusion uses a different clue that is usually right, which is why the brain trusts it.

items.p: Put the steps of the arrow-lines test in order.
items: Measure the copy with a ruler
Draw a 10 cm line with fins
Copy its length by eye from the dot
Write the number in the table
a: Draw a 10 cm line with fins
Copy its length by eye from the dot
Measure the copy with a ruler
Write the number in the table
items.why: First make the test line, then copy it by eye, then measure the copy, then record it.

items.p: Sort these. Is it an illusion, or is it really true?
items: Railway rails seem to meet far away
Illusion
The far end of a corridor seems narrow
Illusion
A pea between crossed fingers feels like two
Illusion
A bus far away makes a small picture in your eye
Really true
Two lines both measure 10 cm with a ruler
Really true
A flip book ball seems to bounce
Illusion
items.a: see items
items.why: The illusions are what the brain makes of the clues. The true ones are what a ruler or a careful test shows. A far bus really does make a small picture in the eye; seeing the bus as small would be the mistake.

items.p: Arjun, a boy in Class 2, says, 'My eyes never get anything wrong.' What would you show him, and what would you say?
items.a: A strong answer names a real test, like the arrow lines or the railway tracks, and says that the eyes caught the light correctly but the brain used a clue and got the length wrong. It ends with measuring to check.
items.why: The point is that illusions happen in the brain's judging, not because the eyes are faulty.

items.p: You copied the open-fin line by eye, and your copy was longer than 10 cm. Why do you think this happened?
items.a: My brain used the open fins as a clue and judged the line to be longer than it is, so I drew it longer.
items.why: A full answer says the fins change how long the line looks, and that the ruler showed the real length.

items.p: Draw the arrow lines: one 6 cm line with arrowheads and one 6 cm line with open fins. Use a ruler. Circle the one that looks longer.
items.a: Two 6 cm lines, one <——> and one >——<. The open-fin line is circled.
items.why: Most people see the open-fin line as longer, though both are 6 cm.
items.art: Two blank rows with a small ruler drawn beside them.

items.p: Label the drawing: eye, optic nerve, brain, and the light coming from a mango.
items.a: The light goes from the mango into the eye. The optic nerve runs from the back of the eye to the brain at the back of the head.
items.why: Seeing needs all of these: light from the thing, the eye to catch it, the nerve to carry signals, and the brain to work out what it means.
items.art: A side view of a child's head looking at a mango, with four blank label lines.

items.p: Two middle circles are drawn round the same bottle cap. One has big circles around it, one has small circles. What will most people say?
opts: The one among small circles looks bigger
The one among big circles looks bigger
items.why: The brain compares a thing with its neighbours. Among small circles, the middle one looks big. This is the Ebbinghaus illusion.

items.p: Max Wertheimer flashed one line, then another line beside it, with a short gap. What did people see?
items.why: People saw one line travelling between the two places, though nothing was there. Blurring would show two lines at once. This showed that the brain makes the movement, not a fading image on the eye.

items.p: Selvi, a girl in Class 3, cut two squares from the same brown envelope. She put one on a black bag and one on white paper. The square on black looked lighter. Why?
opts: The black bag made the square lighter
Her brain judged each square by comparing it with its background
One square had faded in the sun
items.why: Both squares are the same brown. The brain judges how light something is by comparing it with what is next to it. This is called contrast.

items.p: After you measure the arrow lines and know they are equal, the open-fin line stops looking longer.
items.why: False. For almost everyone, the open-fin line still looks longer. Knowing changes what you believe, but it hardly changes what you see.

items.p: Some animals use illusions to stay alive.
items.why: True. Butterflies with eyespots can startle the birds who hunt them, and camouflage helps many animals stay hidden.

items.p: Seeing movement in still pictures shown quickly one after another is called ____ motion.
items.why: 'Apparent' means it seems to be there. The movement is built by the brain.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out? A flip book, a cartoon, a cinema film, a photo on the wall.
items.why: A flip book, a cartoon and a film are still pictures shown quickly one after another, so they seem to move. A photo on the wall is one still picture that stays still.

items.p: Sort these by the clue that fools the brain.
items: Railway strips
Far away
Ring of circles
Neighbours
Grey on black and on white
Neighbours
Shaded bumps
Light from above
Long corridor
Far away
Upside-down footprints in sand
Light from above
items.a: see items
items.why: Far-away clues change how big things look, neighbours change size and brightness by comparing, and light from above changes bumps into dents.

items.p: Put these in order, from first to last, in the story of how we learned why films move.
items: Wertheimer flashes two lines and people see one line move
Films come to cinema halls
Spinning picture toys like the thaumatrope are sold in London
Scientists today say persistence of vision is not the answer
a: Spinning picture toys like the thaumatrope are sold in London
Wertheimer flashes two lines and people see one line move
Scientists today say persistence of vision is not the answer
items.why: The toys came in the 1820s, films in the 1890s, Wertheimer's test in 1912, and today's view after that.

items.p: Match each animal to how illusions help them.
pairs: eyespots that can startle a hungry bird
colours that blend in with branches
a court of stones arranged to look even to a female
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each animal has their own problem: not being eaten, not being seen, or attracting a mate. Each feature helps by acting on another animal's eyes and brain.

items.p: Your copy of the plain line was 10 cm. Your copy of the open-fin line was 12 cm. Why is it useful to have the plain line in the test?
items.a: The plain line shows how well I copy lines anyway. I was right on the plain line, so the extra 2 cm on the open-fin line must come from the fins, not from bad copying.
items.why: This is what makes the test fair: it separates the illusion from ordinary copying mistakes.

items.p: Why do you think the brain uses clues that can sometimes be wrong, instead of measuring everything exactly?
items.a: Clues are fast, and nearly always right. Measuring everything would take far too long to catch a ball, cross a road or run from danger. Getting fooled by a drawing now and then is a small price.
items.why: A strong answer says the clues are usually right and that speed matters for living.

items.p: In the crossed-fingers test, one pea felt like two. Explain why, using the word 'brain'.
items.a: Normally the outer sides of those two fingers never touch the same small thing. When both feel a pea, the brain decides there must be two peas.
items.why: The answer should say the brain uses a map of where the fingers usually are.

items.p: Three people talk about the arrow lines.

views.says: My brain is fooled. The line is 10 cm, and the ruler proves it.
The line really does look longer. What I see is just as real as what the ruler says.
Both are right. The ruler tells you about the line. The seeing tells you about your brain.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason from your own test. Then say one good point about another view.
items.a: A strong answer picks a view and uses evidence, for example: 'Everyone's copy of the plain line was about 10 cm but the open-fin copies were longer, so the fins changed our seeing.' It then gives a fair point for another view, like the grandmother being right that the longer look is a real experience everyone shares.
items.why: The ruler measures the line. The seeing is a real event in each person. Each view says something true.

items.p: Draw a shaded circle that looks like a bump, and one that looks like a dent. Draw a small Sun to show where the light seems to come from.
items.a: The bump is light at the top and dark at the bottom. The dent is dark at the top and light at the bottom. The Sun is drawn above.
items.why: The brain expects light from above, so a surface lit at the top must face up.

items.p: Amma copied the plain line at 9.5 cm, the arrowhead line at 8.5 cm and the open-fin line at 12 cm. How many centimetres did each set of fins change her copy, compared with her plain line?
items.a: Arrowheads made it 1 cm shorter: 9.5 − 8.5 = 1. Open fins made it 2.5 cm longer: 12 − 9.5 = 2.5.
items.why: Comparing with her own plain line, not with 10 cm, takes away her ordinary copying error.

items.p: Kiran says, 'The arrow-lines illusion works because the fins look like corners of a room.' But it still works when the fins are small circles. What does this tell you about Kiran's idea?
items.a: If the illusion still works with circles, which do not look like corners, then the corner idea cannot be the whole reason. Something else, like the brain judging the whole shape's length, must be part of it.
items.why: This is how scientists test an explanation: find a case where it predicts one thing and something else happens.

items.p: Design a test to find out whether practice makes the arrow-lines illusion weaker. Say what you would change, what you would keep the same, and what you would measure.
items.a: Change: how many times the person has done the test (for example day 1, day 2 and day 3). Keep the same: the same 10 cm lines, the same fins, the same way of copying. Measure: how long the open-fin copy is each day.
items.why: A strong answer has one thing that changes, others kept the same, and a measurement.

items.p: A bird is startled by a peacock pansy butterfly's eyespots. Is the bird being foolish? Explain.
items.a: No. For a bird, two big round eyes can mean a predator. A bird who backs away from eye-like shapes is often staying safe. Being wrong about a butterfly costs a meal, but being wrong about a real eye could cost their life.
items.why: A strong answer says the bird's habit is usually useful, just as our brain's clues usually are.

items.p: A book and a scientist disagree about why films seem to move.

views.says: Each picture stays on the eye and blurs into the next. This is persistence of vision.
The brain builds the movement. Wertheimer's two flashed lines looked like one line moving, not two blurred lines.

items.ask: Which explanation fits the two-dot flip book better? Use what you saw. Then say what the old book gets partly right.
items.a: A strong answer says that in the two-dot flip book you see one dot travelling, not two dots at once, which fits the brain building the movement. The old book is partly right that a bright image fades slowly when you shut your eyes.
items.why: A good explanation must fit what really happens. Blurring would show two dots together.

items.p: Three people talk about trusting your eyes.

views.says: I always measure cloth with a tape. My eyes are good, but cloth can fool me.
A batter has no time to measure. She must trust her eyes and brain completely.
We trust our eyes first, then check the important things with a measurement or another person.

items.ask: Whose way would you use when choosing which of two dosas is bigger? Whose way when catching a ball? Explain.
items.a: A strong answer says different jobs need different ways. Catching a ball needs quick trust, like Revathi. Sharing dosas fairly could use a ruler, like Lakshmi. Farah's way joins both.
items.why: The brain's clues are fast and usually right. Measuring is slow but cannot be fooled by fins or neighbours.

items.p: A male great bowerbird lays out stones. Small stones go near the female's spot, bigger ones further away. Why might this help him?
opts: It makes the court look evenly patterned to her
items.why: Scientists Laura Kelley and John Endler found that this forced perspective makes the court look even from where the female watches. Males whose courts made a better illusion mated more often. Exactly why females like it is still being studied.

items.p: You flip between two pages. A dot is on the left of page 1 and on the right of page 2. What do you see?
items.why: The brain joins the two still dots into one moving dot. This is apparent motion, like Wertheimer's flashed lines.

items.p: Which result would show that knowing about the arrow lines does NOT stop the illusion?
opts: After knowing, people copy the open-fin line at exactly 10 cm
After knowing, people still copy it longer than 10 cm
People refuse to do the test again
items.why: If knowing stopped the illusion, the copies would be about 10 cm. Copies still longer than 10 cm show that the seeing kept its own answer.

items.p: In tests in the 1960s, people who grew up with few straight walls and corners were fooled less by the arrow lines.
items.why: True, but they were still fooled, and the groups were different in other ways too, such as schooling. So scientists still argue about what this means.

items.p: A photo can never be an illusion, because a camera does not have a brain.
items.why: False. The camera records the light correctly, but the person looking at the photo uses clues. In a forced perspective photo, the brain is fooled about sizes because the photo hides how far away things are.

items.p: Forced ____ is a trick where near and far things are arranged so their sizes look wrong.
items.why: Photographers and bowerbirds both use forced perspective.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out? The arrow lines, the railway tracks, the ring of circles, crossed fingers and a pea.
items.why: The first three are illusions of seeing size. Crossed fingers and a pea is an illusion of touch.

items.p: Sort these illusions by the sense that is fooled: seeing or touch.
items: Railway strips
Seeing
One pea between crossed fingers
Touch
Shaded bumps and dents
Seeing
A cold, dry steel plate feels wet
Touch
Ring of circles
Seeing
The hole in your hand
Seeing
items.a: see items
items.why: Illusions happen in every sense. In each one, the brain uses a rule that is usually right, such as light coming from above, or where each finger usually is.

items.p: Invent your own illusion using one of the clues: far away, neighbours or light from above. Draw it and write the question you would ask a visitor.
items.a: Any drawing that uses one clue correctly, with a clear question, for example two equal lines between two walls of a corridor drawn in perspective, with the question 'Which person is taller?'.
items.why: A strong answer names the clue and explains why it should fool people.

applications: Films, cartoons and video games show still frames quickly so that we see movement.
Road markings: some cities paint lines closer and closer together before a speed breaker, so drivers feel they are going faster and slow down.
Artists paint flat murals with perspective, so a wall seems to have steps or a window in it.
Photographers and film-makers use forced perspective to make sets and actors look bigger or smaller.
Tailors and clothes designers use stripes and patterns to change how tall or wide clothes look.
Doctors and scientists use illusions to study how the brain works, and to check how vision develops in children.
Running-light signs at shops and railway stations switch bulbs on one after another, so an arrow seems to move.
Camouflage patterns are printed on soldiers' uniforms, copying the way animals hide.

open_questions.q: Why exactly do the arrow lines fool us?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have argued for more than 100 years. The corner idea, the whole-shape idea and others each explain some results but not all.

open_questions.q: Why does the Moon look bigger near the horizon?
open_questions.why_open: Photos show it is the same size, so it is an illusion. Scientists have several explanations about how the brain judges the Moon's distance, but none is agreed.

open_questions.q: How much can what we know change what we see?
open_questions.why_open: Some scientists say knowledge and expectation change seeing a lot. Others say the first stage of seeing works on its own. Experiments give different answers.

open_questions.q: How do our separate guesses about colour, shape, size and movement join into one picture?
open_questions.why_open: Different parts of the brain handle different features. How they come together into one experience is not understood.

open_questions.q: What do other animals see in our illusions?
open_questions.why_open: Some birds, fish and bees respond to some illusions as we do, and not to others. Testing what an animal sees is hard, because they cannot tell us in words.

maths.problem: The real line in the arrow test is 10 cm. Kavya copied the arrowhead line at 8.5 cm. How much too short was her copy?
maths.explain: The real line is 10 cm and Kavya's copy is 8.5 cm. 10 − 8.5 = 1.5. Check by adding: 8.5 + 1.5 = 10. So her copy was 1.5 cm too short.
maths.context: This is about the arrow-lines test. People copy a 10 cm line by eye, and you measure how far off their copy is.
maths.why_maths: Subtracting tells us exactly how much the illusion fooled someone, instead of just saying 'a bit'.

maths.problem: Three people copied the open-fin line. Kavya drew 11.5 cm, Amma 12 cm and Paati 11 cm. The real line is 10 cm. Who was fooled the most, and who the least?
maths.answer: Amma was fooled the most (2 cm too long). Paati was fooled the least (1 cm too long).
maths.explain: Take 10 cm away from each copy. Kavya: 11.5 − 10 = 1.5 cm. Amma: 12 − 10 = 2 cm. Paati: 11 − 10 = 1 cm. 2 is the biggest and 1 is the smallest. But check each person's plain line too. If Amma also copied the plain line too long, part of her 2 cm is ordinary copying.
maths.context: This is about the arrow-lines test, where people copy a 10 cm line with open fins by eye.

chart.title: How much too long each open-fin copy was

maths.why_maths: Ordering the differences lets us compare people fairly, instead of guessing who was fooled more.

maths.problem: In the crossed-fingers test, Revathi got 10 out of 10 right with fingers normal. With fingers crossed she got 6 out of 10 right. How many more did she get wrong with fingers crossed? What fraction of the crossed tries were wrong?
maths.answer: 4 more wrong. 4 out of 10, or 4/10, of the crossed tries were wrong.
maths.explain: Normal: 10 − 10 = 0 wrong. Crossed: 10 − 6 = 4 wrong. 4 − 0 = 4 more. 4 wrong out of 10 tries is the fraction 4/10, which is the same as 2/5.
maths.context: This is about the crossed-fingers test, where one or two peas touch your fingertips while your eyes are shut.
maths.why_maths: A fraction like 4 out of 10 lets us compare tests with different numbers of tries.

maths.problem: A cinema film shows 24 frames every second. How many still pictures does it show in 5 seconds?
maths.explain: 5 seconds of 24 pictures is 5 groups of 24. 24 + 24 + 24 + 24 + 24 = 120. Or 5 × 24 = 120.
maths.context: This is about how films work. A film is many still pictures, called frames, shown one after another.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying shows how many still pictures your brain joins into movement, even in a very short clip.

maths.problem: In the Illusion Museum, 8 visitors looked at each illusion. The arrow lines fooled 7, the railway tracks fooled 6, the ring of circles fooled 5 and the bumps and dents fooled 8. Draw a bar chart. Which illusion fooled everyone?
maths.answer: The bumps and dents fooled all 8 visitors.
maths.explain: Draw one bar for each illusion: 7, 6, 5 and 8. The tallest bar is the bumps and dents at 8, which is every visitor. The ring of circles fooled the fewest, 5.
maths.context: This is about the Illusion Museum project, where you test visitors with illusions you made and count how many each one fooled.
maths.why_maths: A bar chart shows at a glance which illusion is strongest.

roots.context: We have seen equal lines look unequal, still pictures seem to move, and one pea feel like two. Now we ask what illusions tell us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the arrow test, the ruler showed both lines were 10 cm long. Even after you knew, the line with open fins still looked longer. Knowing the answer did not change what you saw. So the part of you that sees can disagree with the part that knows.
deep_truth.habit: We talk as if each of us is one single looker, so that knowing the truth should change what we see. The arrow test shows that seeing keeps its own answer, even while knowing holds another.
deep_truth.evidence: In the arrow test, people still copied the open-fin line longer than 10 cm after the ruler had shown all the lines were 10 cm. Scientists find the same in many illusions: knowing about them hardly weakens them.

three.who_am_i: You are not one single looker. Different parts of your mind work at the same time, and they can give different answers.
three.what_is_life: Every animal's brain judges the world from clues. A great bowerbird even lays out stones to play with a female's sense of distance.
three.what_is_this_world: The world you see is your brain's best judgement from light. A ruler, a test or another person helps you check it.

roots.thread: The same light reaches every eye that looks. Each brain, a bee's, a bowerbird's or yours, builds a picture of that light from the clues it uses. Inside you, too, seeing and knowing each build their own answer. None of these pictures is the whole of what is there. Comparing them, with a ruler or with each other, is how we come closer to it.

teachings.source: Udana 6.4 (Pali Canon), the blind men and the elephant
teachings.teaching: Some men who could not see each touched one part of an elephant. One felt the leg and said an elephant is like a pillar. One felt the ear and said it is like a winnowing basket. Each was sure, and they quarrelled.
teachings.link: Each man's touch gave a true clue but a wrong whole. In an illusion, your eyes give true light, and your brain builds a wrong whole from the clues. Checking with a ruler is like asking the others what they felt.

teachings.teaching: A rope seen unclearly in the dark is taken to be a snake. When the rope is seen for what it is, the snake is gone.
teachings.link: In the rope story, seeing clearly removes the mistake. The arrow lines are different: even after you know the truth, the open-fin line still looks longer. The mistake and the knowing sit side by side.

science.text: Most illusions stay strong after you know about them. Practice weakens the arrow-lines illusion only a little.
How much what we know and expect can change what we see is still argued over.

other_view.who: Scientists who study how expectation shapes seeing
other_view.view: What we know changes what we see all the time. You can read a messy word in a sentence because you expect it. On this view, seeing and knowing are woven together, and the arrow lines are a rare exception, not the rule.

practice.title: Look twice
practice.say: Let's put the arrow lines in front of us. Look at them quietly and breathe slowly, five times. Notice that the open-fin line looks longer. Now lay the ruler on them and read 10 and 10. Look again. Notice that it still looks longer. Say quietly, 'My eyes see one thing. I know another.' Sit with both for three more breaths.
practice.kid: Look at the arrow lines. Breathe slowly five times. One line looks longer. Now measure them. Both are 10 cm. Look again. It still looks longer! Say, 'I see one thing. I know another.'

ask: When the line still looks longer after you have measured it, which answer is yours: the one you see or the one you know?
A bee, a bowerbird and you look at the same garden. Is one of you seeing it right?
If your brain is always judging from clues, how can you check a judgement you do not notice it making?

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if at home, with the materials listed. The arrow-lines test uses A4 paper cut into long strips, because a 10 cm line, its fins, a 4 cm gap and a copy of up to 13 cm need about 29 cm. Each person gets their own strips so nobody copies another person's line. The plain line is in the test so ordinary copying errors can be told apart from the illusion. The 'after knowing' round uses a fresh strip, because copying over an old line would give the answer away. Expect the open-fin copies to be 1 to 3 cm too long and the arrowhead copies 1 to 2 cm too short, with a lot of variation between people. The crossed-fingers test works best with a round dried pea or chana rolled gently. Some children feel one very wide pea instead of two, which still counts as the illusion. Bumps and dents need soft, gradual shading. The grey-squares effect is small, so look from a little distance. The thaumatrope needs the cage drawn upside down to the bird. The hole-in-the-hand trick needs both eyes open. The forced perspective photo needs a grown-up and a safe floor, never a terrace edge. The spine fits about 80 minutes.
